title: What's a catch? Control, feet in bounds and replay (Kent State's overturned TD)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files; it was last updated Oct 12. The original football-film-room repo can't be read from this scheduled run (GitHub access to it isn't enabled). So there are no new misses to target. This lesson adds a new rules concept from Tuesday night's finish, which decided the board's Kent State-EMU bet.

The big idea: a pass is only a catch if three things happen. The receiver controls the ball, gets his feet down in bounds, and (in the NFL) keeps control through the fall.Miss one, and it's incomplete, even if he's holding the ball at the end.Tuesday, Kent State trailed Eastern Michigan 17-12. 4th-and-9 from the EMU 15, 6 seconds left.Wayne Harris was ruled to have caught a winning TD in the back of the end zone. Replay overturned it. EMU won.

Top-down view of the end zone. The yellow line at the back is the end line: stepping on it is out of bounds.

  1. A · Control. The receiver has to secure the ball, not just touch it. A ball that moves around in his hands as he lands isn't controlled yet.
  2. B · Feet in bounds. College needs one foot down in bounds. The NFL needs two feet (or another body part, like a knee).The back of the end zone is the hardest place: the end line is only 10 yards behind the goal line. Harris was catching right at it.
  3. C · Survive the ground (NFL). If an NFL receiver is going to the ground as he catches it, he must keep control after he lands.If the ball pops out when he hits the turf, it's incomplete.
  4. D · Replay. Officials make a call on the field. Replay can only flip it with clear video evidence.In college, every scoring play is reviewed automatically. That's why Kent State's TD got a second look.Sources don't say which part failed on Harris's catch. Officials check A, B and C in that order.
  5. E · Tipped passes are live. When a pass bounces off a player, anyone can still catch it.Same night, Miami (OH)'s Amariyun Knighten caught a deflected pass in the end zone with 26 seconds left. That INT beat Western Michigan 28-24.

Why it matters for bets: a catch at the line can swing a total or a spread with no time left. Kent State's TD would have made it Kent State 18-17 (or 20-17 with a 2-point try).The Under 46.5 was safe either way. But "Kent State +5.5" and "EMU wins" both depended on that replay.

In your drill: your run/pass call is made before the snap, so the rule doesn't change your call.But when you check the result, log a reviewed catch by the final ruling. Kent State's last snap is a "pass, incomplete," not a TD.On 4th-and-9 from the 15 with 6 seconds left, the call is always pass: the clock leaves no time to run (Lesson 34).

Check yourself: an NFL receiver gets one foot down in bounds, then his second foot lands on the end line. Catch? (No. The NFL needs two feet in bounds. In college, one foot would be enough.)

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

quiz.q: How many feet must land in bounds for a college catch?
quiz.w: College needs one foot in bounds. The NFL needs two.

quiz.q: An NFL receiver catches it falling, and the ball pops out when he hits the ground. What's the ruling?
quiz.w: In the NFL a receiver going to the ground must keep control through the landing (C in the diagram).

quiz.q: A pass bounces off the receiver's hands and a defender catches it. What is it?
quiz.w: A tipped pass stays live. Miami (OH)'s Amariyun Knighten made exactly this play to beat WMU.

quiz.q: Replay overturns a TD catch to incomplete. How do you log the snap in your drill?
quiz.w: Log the final ruling. The pre-snap call (pass) was right either way.
